text: Afrmative consent—or “yes means yes”—was initially devised to mitigate sexual violence stemming from misunderstandings of consent. More recently, HCI research has considered adapting afrmative consent to mitigate nonconsensual acts online. Given that afrmative consent has historically been under-adopted and critiqued as unrealistic in its original context of in-person sexual activity, it is imperative that users be involved in producing guidance for afrmative consent practice in computer-mediated contexts. We report a focus group study about afrmative consent in VR dating with 16 stakeholders identifying as women and/or LGBTQIA+ (demographics at elevated risk of nonconsensual acts). Findings suggest that afrmative consent may be obsolete: participants elucidated several reasons why afrmative consent is impractical, if not impossible, to practice in virtual environments. Participants offered provocations to guide creation of new, inherently computermediated consent models for mitigating unwanted acts, posing significant opportunity for HCI to have public health impact.
